cards.explanation: The answer is False. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, asked if seven times was the limit. Jesus told him, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!” (Matthew 18:22). I think Peter was hoping for a high five, and he walked away with homework instead.

The answer is ten thousand talents. The text says, “…a debtor owing ten thousand talents was brought to him.” (Matthew 18:24). Say it slowly, friends, because it's a mountain of a number. I think that debt is meant to feel enormous. That's a long way from pocket change.

The answer is that he's sold, along with his family and everything. The master orders that the man “…be sold to pay his debt, along with his wife and children and everything he owned.” (Matthew 18:25). It's a hard moment, and I think this one hurts. The debt is so big that his whole household is on the line. Hold onto that, because it makes what happens next hit even harder.

The answer is that he falls on his knees and begs. “Then the servant fell on his knees before him. ‘Have patience with me,’ he begged, ‘and I will pay back everything.’” (Matthew 18:26). He doesn't argue or sneak off, he just asks. Remember how that begging sounds, friends, because it comes back around later.

The answer is True. The master forgives all of it. “His master had compassion on him, forgave his debt, and released him.” (Matthew 18:27). The servant had asked for patience and promised to pay it all back. What he got was the whole debt wiped out. I'd have needed a minute to sit down after that.

The answer is False. He does not cancel it. When that servant went out, he grabbed his fellow servant, began to choke him and said, “Pay back what you owe me!” (Matthew 18:28). He had just been forgiven so much. I'd call that a rough turn in the story.

The word is prison. The forgiven servant “…went and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay his debt.” (Matthew 18:30). The fellow servant had begged for patience and promised to pay. It wasn't enough for this man.

The word is master. The text says the fellow servants “…were greatly distressed, and they went and recounted all of this to their master.” (Matthew 18:31). They saw what happened, and they didn't keep it to themselves. Whatever happens next, the master is going to hear all of it.

The answer is that he should have shown his fellow servant mercy the way he was shown mercy. The master asks, “Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?” (Matthew 18:33). It's the same mercy the servant had just been given. The master isn't asking for anything fancy. He's asking him to pass on what he got.

The word is heart. Jesus says, “…unless you forgive your brother from your heart.” (Matthew 18:35). He's pointing at something deeper than the words you say. This is the end of the story, and it's the point He wants Peter and all of us to carry out of the kitchen. It answers Peter's question from the start: forgiveness isn't a number to count.
